title: Erdős #10: Certifying Witnesses by a Finite Offset Search (No native_decide)
description: Resolves the open question left by the Erdős #10 popcount thread: how to certify a concrete witness of 'n is NOT a prime plus ≤ k powers of 2' without native_decide (hence axiom-free, no Lean.ofReduceBool). The shipped decision procedure searches every prime p ≤ n — Θ(n) primality tests, infeasible in the kernel and even for the compiler at n≈10⁹. The fix re-indexes the prime-plus-popcount characterization by the OFFSET m = n−p: IsPrimePlusKPowers k n ↔ ∃ m ≤ n, popcount m ≤ k ∧ (n−m).Prime, whose viable candidates (popcount ≤ k) number only Θ((log n)^k). The contrapositive is the finite refutation criterion ∀ m ≤ n, popcount m ≤ k → ¬(n−m).Prime, a bounded ∀ that the kernel decides. Demonstrated by certifying — axiom-free — that 16 is not a prime plus ≤ 1 power of two (the smallest such witness), the first member of the Erdős #10 witness family proved with no native_decide.

meta.author: Erdős & Graham (problem); Granville–Soundararajan, Grechuk (witnesses); formalized in Lean 4
meta.assumptions: 0 literal `axiom` declarations, 0 sorries, and — the point of the file — NO `native_decide`. `#print axioms` reports only the ordinary foundational axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) for every declaration, including the concrete `16` witness; in particular `Lean.ofReduceBool` is absent. Imports the verified Erdos10WIP01 file (and through it Erdos10OQ02 / Erdos10OQ02Popcount) and reuses `popcount`, `isPrimePlusKPowers_iff_popcount`, `Nat.bitIndices`, `Nat.twoPowSum_bitIndices`, and `Nat.bitIndices_two_pow`.

mathlibDependencies.description: (bitIndices n).map (2^·) |>.sum = n — the binary-expansion identity used to read an offset's value off its bit list
bitIndices (2^k) = [k] — gives popcount(2^a) = 1 without kernel reduction of bitIndices
A prime's only divisors are 1 and itself — the basis of the small-factor compositeness certificate

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #10 asks whether a fixed k makes every large integer a prime plus at most k powers of 2; Erdős and Graham conjectured no such k exists. Concrete witnesses anchor the question: Granville–Soundararajan (1998) conjectured k=3 for odd integers, and Grechuk found that 1117175146 is not a prime plus at most 3 powers of 2. The gallery's Erdos10OQ02 thread reduced 'at most k powers' to k DISTINCT powers, whose minimal count is the binary popcount, and shipped a Decidable instance — but that instance searches every prime p ≤ n, so the witnesses were closed by `native_decide`, which trusts the compiler (the `Lean.ofReduceBool` axiom) and cannot scale to n ≈ 10⁹ anyway. The parent WIP file recorded the open question of certifying such a witness WITHOUT native_decide.
overview.problemStatement: Certify concrete Erdős #10 witnesses ('n is not a prime plus ≤ k powers of 2') by a kernel-checkable, `native_decide`-free procedure — replacing the Θ(n) prime search with a finite search over the offsets m = n−p of binary popcount ≤ k.
overview.text: A 196-line, fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file. Part I re-indexes `isPrimePlusKPowers_iff_popcount` by the offset m = n−p (an involution since n−(n−x)=x), yielding `isPrimePlusKPowers_iff_offset` and its contrapositive `not_isPrimePlusKPowers_iff`, a bounded ∀ over m ≤ n with decidable body. Part II adds `not_prime_of_proper_divisor`: a single small divisor 1<d<q certifies ¬q.Prime in the kernel — the covering-congruence certificate the genuine ~10⁹ witnesses consume. Part III proves the structure lemma `popcount_le_one_iff` (popcount m ≤ 1 ↔ m=0 ∨ m=2^a). Part IV combines them to certify, axiom-free, that 16 is not a prime plus ≤ 1 power of two — the smallest such witness and the first proved with no native_decide.
overview.proofStrategy: The offset reformulation substitutes m = n−p into the prime-indexed characterization `IsPrimePlusKPowers k n ↔ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ p ≤ n ∧ popcount(n−p) ≤ k`; the maps p ↦ n−p and m ↦ n−m are mutually inverse on {· ≤ n} (`Nat.sub_sub_self`), turning the existential over primes into one over offsets of popcount ≤ k. `push_neg` gives the refutation criterion. Because the binary popcount `(Nat.bitIndices ·).length` does NOT reduce under kernel `decide` (only `native_decide` evaluates it), the concrete witness avoids computing popcount: `popcount_le_one_iff` is proved through `Nat.twoPowSum_bitIndices` (so an offset with popcount ≤ 1 is read off as 0 or 2^a), and the witness then bounds the exponent a ≤ 4 and discharges the five compositeness obligations 16−2^a ∈ {15,14,12,8,0} by kernel `decide` on numbers < 16.
keyInsights: Search the OFFSET, not the prime: the witness of a representation is m = n−p, and only offsets with popcount ≤ k can work — there are Θ((log n)^k) of those (≈ 5000 for k=3, n≈10⁹), versus Θ(n) primes below n.

The offset reformulation is an exact equivalence via the involution n−(n−x)=x, so refuting IsPrimePlusKPowers reduces to a bounded ∀ m ≤ n whose body is decidable — kernel-checkable, no native_decide, no Lean.ofReduceBool.

Compositeness for the genuine ~10⁹ witnesses is certified by exhibiting ONE small proper divisor (the covering-congruence prime), not by trial division: `not_prime_of_proper_divisor` is the kernel-fast tool.

Binary popcount does not reduce under kernel `decide`, so popcount facts must come from structure lemmas (popcount ≤ 1 ↔ 0 or a power of two), not computation — the reason the original thread needed native_decide.
16 is the smallest integer not a prime plus ≤ 1 power of two, now certified axiom-free; contrast the shipped 906 / 1117175146 facts, which carry Lean.ofReduceBool via native_decide.
prerequisites: Binary representation / Nat.bitIndices and the kernel-vs-compiler distinction (decide vs native_decide)

sections.title: Header: Kernel-Decidable Witnesses via Offset Search
sections.summary: Module docstring: identifies the gap in the parent's decidability route — searching all Θ(n) prime candidates forces native_decide (not axiom-free) for n≈10⁹ witnesses — and states the fix: reindexing by the offset m=n−p restricts the search to the Θ((log n)^k) offsets with popcount m≤k, yielding a bounded-∀ refutation criterion checkable by kernel decide with no native_decide.
sections.mathContext: Offset reformulation: $\mathrm{IsPrimePlusKPowers}(k,n) \iff \exists m\le n,\ \mathrm{popcount}(m)\le k \wedge (n-m).\mathrm{Prime}$, giving the kernel-decidable refutation $\neg\mathrm{IsPrimePlusKPowers}(k,n) \iff \forall m\le n,\ \mathrm{popcount}(m)\le k \to \neg(n-m).\mathrm{Prime}$ — a bounded $\forall$ over $\Theta((\log n)^k)$ candidates instead of $\Theta(n)$ primality tests.

conclusion.summary: Resolves the parent's open question by supplying the missing decision architecture: re-index the Erdős #10 predicate by the offset m = n−p so that refuting a witness becomes a finite, kernel-decidable ∀ over offsets of bounded popcount, and certify each compositeness obligation by a single small divisor. The smallest concrete witness — 16 is not a prime plus ≤ 1 power of two — is proved axiom-free (no native_decide, no Lean.ofReduceBool), the first member of the Erdős #10 witness family with that status.
conclusion.implications: The offset reformulation is the practical engine for native_decide-free witness certification at any scale: for Grechuk's 1117175146 it reduces the claim to ≈ 5000 compositeness obligations, each dischargeable by not_prime_of_proper_divisor once the covering-congruence factor table (a finite (offset, small prime) data set) is supplied. The proof obligations are all in place; only the data table remains, moving the 10⁹ witness from a native_decide black box to an auditable, axiom-free certificate.
openQuestions: Assemble the covering-congruence factor table for 1117175146 (≈ 5000 (offset, small prime divisor) pairs) and feed it to not_isPrimePlusKPowers_iff + not_prime_of_proper_divisor for a fully axiom-free certificate of Grechuk's witness.
Prove the analogous popcount_le_two_iff / popcount_le_three_iff structure lemmas so the offset enumeration for k = 2 (smallest witness 906) and k = 3 closes by the same native_decide-free route.
